title: The Samaritan woman (John 4:1–26)
hook: a well, a thirsty Jew, a woman with five husbands, and worship in spirit and truth

segments.voice: Yesterday, John the Baptist watched the crowds drift toward Jesus and called himself the friend of the bridegroom, glad to fade. Your line was he must increase. Who did you let shine? Day six hundred two.

Noon. The hottest hour. A well outside a Samaritan town called Sychar, and a tired man sitting on the edge of it, alone, because his friends have gone to buy food. John says it plainly: "Jesus therefore, being wearied with his journey, sat thus on the well: and it was about the sixth hour." The sixth hour is midday. Nobody draws water at midday if they can help it. Then a woman comes with her jar. And the tired man, a Jewish teacher in Samaritan country, does something that breaks about three rules at once. He asks her for a drink.

She's as surprised as anyone: "How is it that thou, being a Jew, askest drink of me, which am a woman of Samaria? for the Jews have no dealings with the Samaritans." Jews and Samaritans were neighbors who shared the five books of Moses but had argued for centuries about where God should be worshiped: Jerusalem, or Mount Gerizim, the mountain right above this well. Jesus answers with a riddle about water. If you knew who was asking, you'd have asked him, and he'd have given you living water. In Greek, living water is also the ordinary phrase for running water, fresh from a spring, so she takes him literally. You don't even have a bucket, she says. Then he turns the talk to her life. Go, call your husband. I have no husband, she says. True, he answers: you've had five, and the man you're with now isn't your husband. Preachers have often called her a sinner. The text never says why she had five husbands. Widowhood, divorce, a man's decision: in her world, a woman rarely chose. John is silent, and some readers now hear in her story more loss than scandal. What she does next is remarkable. She doesn't run. She asks the oldest question between their peoples: which mountain is the right one? And Jesus says an hour is coming when it won't be this mountain or Jerusalem. "God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth." Then he says plainly who he is. "I that speak unto thee am he." Many readers count this as the longest conversation Jesus has with anyone in this Gospel, and it's with her. This week we've sat under a fig tree, tasted the best wine last, watched a temple turned into a body, heard about wind and a new birth, God so loving the world, a friend glad to fade, and now a well at noon.
screen: then, large: `IN SPIRIT AND IN TRUTH.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: worship without a building today. Wherever you are right now is the well. A kitchen, a car, a bench. Settle, and breathe. Notice that nothing about this place is holy in the usual way. Then let the two words sit with you. Spirit: what's alive in you right now, under the noise. Truth: one honest thing about your life you'd usually leave out. If you pray, you can bring both, just as they are, to God, here, without a church around you. If you don't, simply be honest and awake for these minutes. The bell holds the time.
The Samaritan woman. Unnamed in John, she has one of Jesus's longest conversations in the Gospel, and hears him say plainly who he is.
Your line: in spirit and in truth. Today, find one ordinary place, a sink or a sidewalk, and treat it as a place where God can be met. Day six hundred two, and another week on the path.

howItsDone: Christians read this story in many churches during Lent; the Orthodox Church honors the woman as Saint Photini, and her conversation is often used to teach that worship isn't bound to one place.

original.note: Greek: living water. In everyday speech, it meant fresh running water from a spring.

trapdoor: what you thought: a story about a sinful woman Jesus forgave.
what it means: a long, serious conversation across a deep divide, ending with Jesus saying plainly who he is.
what a scholar hears: "living water" is a pun on running water, and John never explains the five husbands, so the scandal may be more ours than the text's.

notes: Index carry 'in spirit and in truth' matches KJV 4:24.
Claim that this is Jesus's longest recorded conversation in John: widely stated; confirm against Nicodemus (3:1–21) and the Farewell Discourse (which is largely monologue).

Claim that John 4:26 is the first time in John that Jesus plainly says who he is: removed from voice in review (debated; cf. 1:51, 3:13–14); 'longest conversation' softened to 'many readers count' in voice, word and myth. Confirm.
'Living water' as an idiom for running/spring water: standard in commentaries. Confirm.
Reading of the five husbands as possible loss rather than scandal is presented as 'some readers'. Confirm fair balance.
Orthodox tradition names her Photini; confirm for howItsDone.
